Familial cerebral cavernous malformation (FCCM) is an autosomal dominant disease induced by loss-of-function mutations in three CCM genes, KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10. However, previous studies paid little attention to analyzing the radiologic features and age-related disease burden according to the genes. Therefore, we retrospectively reviewed the genetic tests of our center's clinical FCCM patients.

Among the patients (n = 34) undergoing the FCCM gene test, twenty-seven patients had CCM confirmed by brain MRI, and twenty-one patients were considered to have FCCM (cohort 1). In cohort 1, thirteen patients had mutations in the FCCM gene, but eight did not. Cohort 2 comprised cohort 1 and four family members with the same mutation as the probands. Six novel variants in CCM genes were detected (KRIT1 c.22_26del, c.815dup, c.1094_1098del, c.1147-2A>G, c.2124dup, and PDCD10 c.150 + 1dup). Cohort 1 demonstrated that brainstem lesions were mostly associated with the mutation detection in CCM genes (brainstem, lateral temporal, and parietal lesions vs. lateral temporal and parietal lesions, AUC 0.928 vs. 0.779, P = 0.0389). The radiologic severity worsened according to age in the KRIT1 group compared with the Mutation not detected group (correlation coefficient 0.75 (P < 0.001) versus 0.53 (P = 0.004)).

Cerebral cavernous malformation (CCM) is an intracranial vascular malformation causing a collection of abnormally distended capillaries. 1 CCM is broadly divided into sporadic and familial categories. Familial CCM (FCCM) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in three genes, KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10. In contrast to sporadic CCM patients, who typically have a solitary lesion, FCCM patients present with multiple CCM lesions showing progressive increases in number and size. The pathophysiology of CCM has recently been elucidated, and various mechanisms associated with the development and hemorrhage have been suggested. 2 These prior studies demonstrated that the products of the three genes (KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10) are associated with CCM form complexes. Loss of function (LOF) of these genes leads to the formation of CCM. Despite the tremendous progress in understanding CCM, the explicit mechanisms underlying the vascular-specific manifestation and vascular malformation suppression of the three CCM genes remain unknown. Understanding variants in the CCM-associated genes could help explain the function of CCM complexes and their interaction with other proteins. 3 Hence, genetic testing for those suspected to be FCCM could be important. While many variants have been reported, studies on Korean FCCM patients are sparse. 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 Furthermore, previous studies paid little attention to analyzing the radiologic features and age-related disease burden according to the genes. We examined the manifestations of Korean FCCM patients and their CCM gene test results and evaluated the clinical and radiologic features associated with these mutations. In addition, the disease burden of FCCM according to age was analyzed.

section: Body / Methods / Clinical data and brain imaging
context: We investigated the patients' clinical manifestations, including demographics, symptoms, presence of spinal cavernous malformation (CM) and cutaneous CM, history of cavernous angioma with symptomatic hemorrhage (CASH), brain surgery due to CCM, radiotherapy for other reasons, and tumors. We only reviewed brain MRIs, including T1-weighted imaging (T1WI), T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), and axial susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or gradient echo imaging (GRE). For analysis, a total of eighty brain MRIs were conducted, and 20% (16/80) and 80% (64/80) were MRIs with GRE and SWI sequences, respectively. The last MRIs in all patients contained SWI sequences. For recording the location, we used the SWI because of its high sensitivity. However, we included not the lesions, which were only visible on SWI, but the lesions frankly visible on T1WI and T2WI (i.e., non-Zabramski type IV).

We only reviewed brain MRIs, including T1-weighted imaging (T1WI), T2-weighted imaging (T2WI), and axial susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) or gradient echo imaging (GRE). For analysis, a total of eighty brain MRIs were conducted, and 20% (16/80) and 80% (64/80) were MRIs with GRE and SWI sequences, respectively. The last MRIs in all patients contained SWI sequences. For recording the location, we used the SWI because of its high sensitivity. However, we included not the lesions, which were only visible on SWI, but the lesions frankly visible on T1WI and T2WI (i.e., non-Zabramski type IV).

section: Body / Methods / Clinical data and brain imaging
context: To evaluate the burden of CCMs, we did not use the total number of CCMs because the number of tiny lesions could be easily affected by image protocol and section. Instead, we counted the number of large CCMs (i.e., those ≥5 mm in diameter). Because of blooming artifacts in SWI and GRE, lesion size measurement was based on T2WI. We investigated the trajectory of the number of large CCMs, defined as larger than or equal to 5 mm, measured by T2WI, according to age. Two or more brain MRIs within six months were considered same-period imaging.

section: Body / Methods / DNA extraction, sequencing, and analysis
context: Patient blood samples were acquired, and DNA was extracted from the samples. For the detection of the variants in the KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10 genes, hybridization capture-based next-generation sequencing (NGS) was performed, and the sequences were aligned to the reference sequences [KRIT1 (NG_012964.1/NC_000007.14), CCM2 (NG_016295.1/NC_000007.14), and PDCD10 (NG_008158.1/NC_000003.12)]. The pathogenicity of each variant was determined according to the guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) 2015. 8 We used the human gene mutation database (HGMD) for a mutation database. Moreover, The Genome Aggregation Database (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/) and the Korean Reference Genome database (http://152.99.75.168/KRGDB/) were used as population references. For the in silico analysis of altered splicing, we used FSPLICE, NNSplice, and NetGene2.

We summarized the clinical data as percentages or means and standard deviations. To compare the differences between the two groups, Mutation detected and Mutation not detected, we utilized the Mann-Whitney U or Student's t test for continuous variables and the chi-square or Fisher's exact test for categorical variables. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis for predicting mutation detection by the specific CCM locations was performed using a logistic regression model and the calculated propensity score. To compare two ROC curves, the DeLong test was used. We used Cox proportional hazards models to estimate the probability of first cavernous angiomas with the occurrence of symptomatic hemorrhage (CASH) between birth and various ages. Moreover, we determined whether CCM genotype was associated with the earlier occurrence of the first CASH, adjusting for gender and first CCM diagnosis age using Cox proportional hazards models. To evaluate the change in large CCM numbers according to the age, we used Pearson's correlation test when the variables were normally distributed or Spearman's rank correlation test when they were not. All analyses were performed using SPSS 26.0 and R version 4.2.1, and a scatter plot was created using RStudio. A P-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Seoul National University approved this Korean familial cerebral cavernous malformation study (H-2204-163-1320). Because this study was retrospective, the IRB exempted informed consent, and information from medical records was deidentified for the subjects' privacy.

A total of thirty-four patients underwent the CCM gene test. (Fig. 1) However, seven patients with multiple lesions were excluded because the lesions were regarded as non-CCM lesions, including cerebral microbleeds in small vessel disease (n = 5), diffuse axonal injury (n = 1), and multiple and recurrent intracerebral hemorrhages without CCM lesions (n = 1) by neuroradiologists. Of the remaining 27 patients, six sporadic CCM patients with a wild-type FCCM gene, a single CCM lesion, and no family history of CCM were excluded. The twenty-one FCCM patients were divided into two groups: thirteen patients with pathogenic variants in CCM genes and eight patients with undetected mutations. The eight patients had multiple lesions suggestive of FCCM. All (n = 21) of the patients considered to be FCCM (gene confirmed or clinical) were analyzed for clinical manifestation and radiologic findings (cohort 1). Furthermore, four family members of three probands underwent a family gene test and had the same mutation as the proband. The data of twenty-five patients, combining cohort 1 with the familial members, were used for the analysis of the age-related disease burden in FCCM (cohort 2). There was neither a patient with a developmental venous anomaly nor a history of radiation in our cohort.

Cohort 1 consisted of nine patients with KRIT1 variants, two with CCM2 variants, two with PDCD10 variants, and eight with the mutation not detected (Table 1). In Table 1, clinical characteristics and imaging findings are described according to All, KRIT1, CCM2, PDCD10, Mutation detected, and Mutation not detected groups. The mean diagnosis ages of the overall and the last brain MRI were 36.8 (standard deviation, SD 18.5) and 45.0 (SD 18.5) years old, respectively. There was a slight female predominance (male: female = 38.1:61.9). A total of 90.5% of the patients were symptomatic, and seizures were the most common manifestation. Moreover, the mean age of seizure onset was 34.5 (SD 19.5) years. CASH occurred in 52.4% of the patients overall; the mean age of CASH was 29.4 (SD 18.8) years old, and the mean number of CASH events was 1.8 (SD 1.3). Overall, 33.3% of the patients underwent surgery for CASH or enlarged symptomatic CCM lesions. A total of 42.9% of the overall patients had a family history. However, the rate was inaccurate because the family history of CCM was usually obtained by history taking. Meanwhile, the lesions were distributed over various locations. The frequencies were lower in the basal ganglia (9.5%) and thalamus (42.9%) than in the other sites.

section: Body / Result / Comparison of the Mutation detected and Mutation not detected groups
context: Even though there was no statistical significance in the clinical characteristics, some conditions were relatively disproportionate. While the gender ratio of Mutation detected was neutral, Mutation not detected demonstrated a female predominance. In the Mutation detected group, the prevalence of seizures was relatively higher (46.2%), and the age of seizure onset was younger (29.0 years old, SD 19.7) than in the Mutation not detected group (25.0%; 51.0 years old, SD 2.8). The Mutation not detected group had a lower frequency of family history. However, as mentioned above, the difference could result from the detection bias.

context: Comparison of two receiver operating curves predicting the detection of CCM gene mutation. The prediction model for the detection of CCM gene mutations was derived from the presence of lesions at specific anatomical sites (brainstem, lateral temporal, and parietal lobe), which were associated with mutation detection. The three new models were generated to investigate the site most relevant to mutation detection by removing each predicting factor (brainstem, lateral temporal lobe, or parietal lobe) from the original models. Subtracting the presence of brainstem lesions significantly reduced the area under the curve. context: In cohort 2 (n = 25), combining cohort 1 with the four family members, the mean number of brain MRIs with the appropriate protocol (mentioned above) was 3.2 per person (80 brain MRIs/25 patients). The mean interval between the first and last MRI was 3.42 years (SD 4.69). Eight patients underwent only one brain MRI. In the patients with at least two MRIs, the mean rate of the large lesion (≥5 mm) number change was 1.18/year (SD 1.97/year). Besides, the cumulative incidence rate of the first CASH was 0.160 until nineteen years old (Table S2). The risk of first CASH did not show a plateau as the patients got older. The difference among the CCM mutation genotypes was not statistically significant (Table S3). The patients diagnosed at a younger age were at increased risk of the earlier first CASH. To exhibit the age-related disease burden of FCCM, we investigated the number of large CCMs by age (Fig. 3A). The correlation coefficient was 0.27 (p = 0.017). In addition, the data were analyzed according to four groups (Mutation not detected, KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10). (Fig. 3B) Eighteen patients (seven Mutation not detected, six KRIT1, two CCM2, and three PDCD10 patients) underwent at least two brain MRIs, and seven (one Mutation not detected, four KRIT1, and two PDCD10 patients) underwent only one brain MRI. The correlation coefficients of the KRIT1, Mutation not detected, and CCM2 groups were 0.75 (P < 0.001), 0.53 (P = 0.004), and - 0.84 (p = 0.019), respectively. However, the correlation between age and the number of large CCMs was not statistically significant in the PDCD10 group.

The proportions of CCM genes (KRIT1 69.2%, CCM2 15.4%, and PDCD10 15.4%) affected were similar to those in previous reports. 12 However, the patients without detected mutations accounted for a larger proportion (38.1%) of our cohort, in contrast to previous cohorts in which mutations were undetected in >5% of the patients. These patients had at least five lesions and no history of head, neck, or intracranial radiation, suggesting clinical FCCM. There are several reasons that mutations were not detected. First, intronic variants or copy number variations in KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10 could not be detected by our DNA sequencing method. In fact, large deletion/duplication mutations, such as deletions spanning exons 2-10, accounted for 30-60% of CCM2 variants despite a low proportion (approximately 20%) of CCM2 variants. 13 , 14 Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification and whole genome sequencing are needed to identify these variants. Second, other gene mutations could induce FCCM despite the rarity of the disease. F. Gianfrancesco et al. proposed that ZPLD1 mutation is associated with FCCM. 15 Furthermore, various genes related to CCM pathophysiology were recently discovered. 2 In the 2-hit model, biallelic LOF in CCM genes, achieved by one somatic mutation in heterozygous germline mutation or two somatic mutations in wild-type gene, is required to initiate CCM formation. Moreover, gain-of-function (GOF) mutations in MAP3K3, encoding MEKK3, have been confirmed in sporadic CCM patients. 16 LOF in CCM genes and GOF in MAP3K3 are mutually exclusive, and the researchers suggested that CCM complexes suppress the activity of MEKK3. Therefore, the mutation of these genes could be a novel cause of FCCM. Finally, multiple sporadic CCMs are possible but rare.

In our cohort, six novel variants were confirmed, despite the limitations of a single-center study. Three case reports of Korean FCCM have been published to date, and four variants (KRIT1 c.535C>T, p. Arg179*; c.816delG, p. Arg273Glufs*; c.940_943 del, p. Val314 Asn315delinsThrfs*3; PDCD10 c.103C>T, p. Arg35*) were documented. 5 , 6 , 7 KRIT1 c. 535C>T, p. Arg179* was also identified in our cohort. When our cohort was combined with previously reported variants, the mutations were located at KRIT1 exons 1, 4, 5, 6, 8, 11,13, intervening sequence (IVS) 8, CCM2 exons 2 and 6, and PDCD10 exons 2, 4, and IVS 2. In particular, the KRIT1 IVS8 variant (c.1147-2A>G), a canonical splice site mutation, was expected to induce exon skipping of exon 12 and an in-frame mutation. Exon 12 is responsible for a particular portion of the KRIT1 protein ankyrin component. 19 This component is likely critical for preventing vascular malformation. Two probands had this mutation and showed different clinical manifestations, including age at diagnosis and the presence of CASH.

On the analysis of age-related disease burden, the large lesions (>5 mm) increased in number as the patient's age increased. Because genetic information was scarce in the previous analysis of FCCM, 20 we investigated the change in CCM lesion counts according to CCM genes and age. Although the patients in the Mutation not detected and KRIT1 groups tended to be diagnosed at an older age, the severity of brain imaging worsened faster in the KRIT1 group than in the Mutation not detected group. CCM2 variant patients are usually asymptomatic and have milder symptoms. 9 However, the CCM2 group exhibited an early diagnosis with a CASH event, albeit with a decreased lesion number over time. These confusing findings might result from detection bias, in which many asymptomatic patients with the CCM2 variant did not visit the hospital and were not diagnosed or enrolled. PDCD10 variant patients usually have early onset and severe manifestations. 12 Even if the correlation was not statistically significant, the PDCD10 group trended toward early onset. Additionally, a patient with infancy onset had recurrent CASH with a short interval, resulting in a very poor prognosis.

Our study has some limitations. First, it is a single-center study. To thoroughly evaluate the Korean FCCM population, a multicenter study is needed in Korea. Second, our center is a tertiary hospital where patients with severe symptoms are likely to be enrolled. In addition, the sample size was too small to draw a definite conclusion. A future study with a large sample size is warranted. Last, we could not use the total lesion counts because of the variability in the imaging protocol. However, Christine K. Fox et al. revealed that large CCM lesion (a least 5 mm) counts are more associated with early-onset seizure than total lesion counts. 11

This study was larger than previous Korean FCCM studies and revealed six novel variants in CCM genes. Furthermore, we propose that the FCCM gene panel, including KRIT1, CCM2, and PDCD10, can be recommended when brainstem lesions are confirmed in patients with multiple lesions suspected to have FCCM. Last, we demonstrated the age-related disease burden of FCCM, in which the burden of the KRIT1 group was aggravated faster than that of the Mutation not detected group, and the PDCD10 group had a tendency toward early onset.
